implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: a carrier type plus two things - a distinguished identity value and an associative combine - and a single generic fold that walks any collection of those values using only those two. Write the laws down (identity on both sides, associativity) and test them with a property-based checker before the instance is used. State explicitly whether the operation is also commutative: associativity licenses regrouping, not reordering, and conflating the two is the most common way a lawful-looking instance turns out to be wrong on skewed input.
idiom_name: carrier type + identity element + associative combine, consumed by one generic fold
code_sketch:
def concat(xs):
    acc = identity          # e.g. b'' for bytes, set() for a set, [] for a list
    for x in xs:
        acc = combine(acc, x)   # associative: regrouping is safe
    return acc              # total: the empty fold yields the identity

# the two laws, as properties
#   combine(identity, x) == x == combine(x, identity)
#   combine(combine(a, b), c) == combine(a, combine(b, c))
# state clearly whether combine is ALSO commutative (reordering) - usually it is not
pitfalls: Associativity permits regrouping, not reordering; a commutative-looking instance for an order-sensitive operation is wrong exactly when the data is skewed.
A combine that is O(n) per call makes the whole fold quadratic even though the fold looks linear.
An identity that is observable (a leading separator, an empty element in a set) leaks an artefact of the algebra into the domain.
